title: manila like local 2026 08 29
text:
The first things you notice when you arrive in Manila are the traffic, the clinging heat and the constant noise. It can feel overwhelming initially, with streets that rarely seem to slow down.
But stay a little longer, and something else begins to emerge. Manila is not just a city of congestion and chaos. It is also a place of warm welcomes, lively street life and food that draws people together. Beneath the frenetic pace is a city shaped by centuries of history, with neighbourhoods still anchored by Spanish churches and cobblestone streets worn down by time and footsteps, where conversations linger and weekend escapes to beaches and mountains are never far away.
I was born in the Philippines and have spent two decades covering the country for Reuters — its economic cycles, its political upheavals and its navigation of its place in an increasingly tense region. What emerges is a city that can be rough and uneven, yes, but also layered and beautiful.
Here’s how to experience Manila like a local:
The way around: I love to cycle, but Manila often has other ideas. This is not a city known for its bike lanes, and public transport can be patchy and unpredictable. You learn to adapt.
The most iconic transport option is the jeepney, a colourful, open-sided minibus also known as the "King of the Road," and a symbol of Filipino ingenuity. They’re cheap and ubiquitous — fares start at around 14 pesos ($0.22), if you don’t mind the heat and sitting shoulder to shoulder with strangers.
For more predictable trips, there’s Grab, the ride-hailing app that has become a go-to for many professionals despite the higher cost. The Light Rail Transit and Metro Rail Transit offer a faster way to cut through the traffic, connecting Manila with neighbouring cities in the capital region, though trains can be crowded during peak hours.
Things to see: One of the bestplaces to begin your exploration is Intramuros, the old walled city that served as the seat of Spanish colonial power in the heart of the capital. Its centuries-old churches, stone fortifications and cobblestone streets offer a glimpse into Manila's colonial past.
From there, continue to Binondo, the world’s oldest Chinatown, where commerce hums alongside a wide array of Chinese dishes, noodle shops, dim sum restaurants, and bakeries selling steamed pork buns, sweet bean-filled pastries and spring rolls in a way that feels both ancient and entirely present.
A few streets away stands Quiapo Church, home to the revered "Black Nazarene" statue of Christ, whose annual January procession draws millions of devotees in one of the largest expressions of Catholic faith in Asia. Not far away is Rizal Park, popularly known as Luneta, where the imposing monument to national hero José Rizal — whose writings helped inspire the movement that led to the Philippine Revolution in the 1890s against Spanish rule — stands watch over the city.
Across the park lies the National Museum Complex, home to archaeological treasures, ethnographic collections and some of the country's most important works of art, including Juan Luna's "Spoliarium," a monumental 19th-century painting depicting fallen gladiators being dragged from a Roman arena. A couple of kilometres away, overlooking the Pasig River, you'll find Malacañang Palace, the official residence and workplace of the Philippine president, originally built during the Spanish colonial era.
For a glimpse of Manila at its most frenetic, head to Divisoria, a sprawling wholesale and retail market packed with malls, street stalls and warehouses. Here, shoppers weave through crowds in search of bargains on everything from clothes and shoes to party supplies, decorations, household goods and gadgets, with goods including low-cost imports and locally made products.
The definitive food item: If you’ve spent any time on food shows or travel blogs, you’ve likely come across adobo, the Philippines’ most recognisable dish. At its simplest, it is pork or chicken braised in vinegar, soy sauce, garlic, peppercorns and bay leaves, creating a balance of sour and savoury flavours. It is also forgiving: even someone like me, who rarely cooks, can make a decent adobo. For a restaurant version, many locals swear by Manam's.
Then there is balut, a fertilised duck egg with a partially developed embryo, often eaten straight from the shell on the street. It has appeared on TV shows like “Fear Factor” because of how it looks, but locals see it as a protein-rich snack, best enjoyed warm with salt or vinegar.
Even outsiders might be familiar with Jollibee, the homegrown fast-food giant where crispy Chickenjoy, sweet-style spaghetti and peach mango pie have become comfort-food staples across generations.
To wash it down, there is fresh coconut juice sold on street corners, scooped straight from the shell and served over ice, with tender coconut meat included. For runners like me, it is the perfect recovery drink.
For dessert, try halo-halo, which literally means “mix-mix,” a concoction of sweetened beans, jellies and fruit layered beneath shaved ice, milk, caramel custard and purple yam. My personal favourite is found at Razon's, whose pared-down version proves that less can sometimes be more. Others recommend Bebang's, which uses frozen milk instead of shaved ice.
Dress like a local: In Manila’s heat and humidity, breathable fabrics are essential. Cotton remains a reliable choice and on any given day you will see cotton shirts paired with shorts or loose trousers, although many locals have also embraced modern technical textiles. Local brands BENCH/ and Penshoppe are everywhere, offering affordable everyday clothing. Footwear tends toward the practical — I usually opt for sneakers, which are best for Manila’s uneven sidewalks.
If you really want to fit in, carry an umbrella — useful as much for shade as for the sudden downpours.
Getting away: A two- or three-hour drive out of the city takes you to beaches, mountains and cooler air.
In Batangas, 66 miles (107 km) south of Manila, the water clears and the pace slows. Diving spots around Anilao attract everyone from beginners to seasoned divers for their vibrant coral reefs and sea turtles. One of its best-known sites is The Cathedral, which features an underwater cross surrounded by reef fish.
Or head to Tagaytay, perched on a ridge overlooking Taal Volcano — one of the world’s smallest active volcanoes, which sits on an island in the middle of a lake. The city has become a food destination, known for bulalo, a rich beef marrow soup, tawilis, a freshwater sardine found only in Taal Lake, and buko (coconut) pie, a regional staple. Cafes make the most of the breeze.
For something more active, hike up Mount Makiling, a volcano steeped in folklore, or ride the rapids at Pagsanjan Falls.
CITY MEMO DATA POINTS
Population: 1.9 million
Price of a cup of coffee: 15 pesos ($0.24) for a black coffee from a roadside stall, poured from a thermos. For something a step up but distinctly Filipino, head to Bo’s Coffee, which champions local beans, or Figaro, a long-time fixture of the café scene. Newer chains such as But First, Coffee reflect how quickly Manila’s coffee culture is evolving, with most drinks costing less than 300 pesos ($4.50).
Price of an ice cream scoop: 10-20 pesos ($0.16-0.32) for a scoop from roaming ice cream vendors pushing colourful carts and referred to as Mamang Sorbetero. The name comes from sorbetes, a traditional Filipino frozen dessert, and “mamang,” a familiar way of referring to an older man. They sell coconut-based ice cream, churned the old-fashioned way and served in flavours such as cheese, chocolate, ube and mango. For something more artisan, Manila Creamery offers Filipino-inspired flavours such as ube, tablea and durian for 120-160 pesos ($1.95-$2.60) per scoop.
Great place to see a sunset: Manila Bay — sitting at a café on Roxas Boulevard, walking the bay front, or looking out from a hotel balcony.
Oldest university: University of Santo Tomas, founded in 1611 and now home to more than 40,000 students.
